analysis.one_liner: Imposes uniform federal rules on product liability lawsuits, limiting punitive damages and shielding FDA-approved drugs and FAA-certified planes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in May 1993 and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 [S1][S5].
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the fifty states' own product liability laws with a single federal rulebook for lawsuits over injury caused by products [S2][S3]. It set a uniform two-year time limit for filing suit, capped and restricted punitive damages, made each defendant pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering awards, and gave manufacturers a complete defense when the injured person was more than half at fault because of alcohol or drugs [S3]. It also barred punitive damages against FDA-approved drugs and FAA-certified aircraft, and reduced any court award by the workers' compensation benefits the injured worker receives [S3]. The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in committee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of consumer and industrial products, who would face shorter deadlines, tighter standards for suing them, and lower exposure to large jury awards. Drug makers and aircraft manufacturers gain the most: as long as regulators approved their product and they disclosed information honestly, they could not be hit with punitive damages at all [S3]. Insurers and business defendants also gain from settlement rules that penalize plaintiffs who reject offers and then win less at trial [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Product manufacturers, drug and aircraft makers, insurers

how_it_helps.text: Sets a uniform two-year deadline for filing product injury lawsuits, running from when the person discovered the harm and its cause [S2][S3].

Caps punitive damages behind a 'clear and convincing evidence' standard requiring proof of conscious, flagrant indifference to safety, and bars them entirely against FDA-approved drugs, FDA-approved medical devices, and FAA-certified aircraft unless the company misled the regulator or bribed an official [S3].

Limits liability of non-manufacturer sellers (retailers, distributors) to cases of their own negligence or breach of their own express warranty, instead of the stricter seller liability many states imposed [S2][S3].

Makes each defendant pay only its own percentage share of pain-and-suffering damages rather than being jointly responsible for the whole award, and lets any defendant force the punitive damages question into a separate proceeding after the main verdict [S3].
Reduces any damages award by the workers' compensation benefits the injured worker is or would be entitled to receive [S2][S3].
Gives manufacturers and sellers a complete defense if the injured person was under the influence of alcohol or non-prescribed drugs and was more than 50 percent responsible for the event [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products. They would face a shorter filing window, lose the ability to collect a full judgment when a solvent defendant and an insolvent one share fault, see their recoveries reduced by workers' compensation benefits, and lose any punitive damages claim against an approved drug or certified aircraft. State laws giving consumers stronger remedies would be overridden [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt stronger state consumer-protection laws, so an injured person in a state with a longer filing period or broader seller liability would lose those rights [S2][S3].

The punitive damages shield for FDA-approved drugs and FAA-certified aircraft relies entirely on regulators doing their job correctly; a product approved on incomplete or mistaken review could injure many people with no punitive penalty available, and the exception applies only where the company withheld or misrepresented information to the agency [S3].

Several liability means that if two defendants share fault and one cannot pay, the injured person absorbs the shortfall, because each defendant pays only its own percentage of pain-and-suffering damages [S3].

Damages are reduced by the full amount of workers' compensation benefits, including future benefits, which can leave an injured worker with little or nothing beyond the workers' compensation system itself [S3].

A good-faith supporter would acknowledge the uniform federal standard trades away state-level protections that were often the only check on dangerous products, in exchange for predictability for businesses [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real benefits to businesses: one predictable national rulebook instead of fifty state systems, faster settlements, and relief from outsized jury awards. But those benefits came directly out of the pockets of people hurt by defective products, through shorter deadlines, reduced awards, and near-total immunity from punitive damages for regulated drugs and aircraft. On balance the bill's gains flowed to manufacturers and insurers while its costs fell on injured consumers, and it died without ever reaching a vote [S2][S3][S5].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees in May 1993, split between two subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Toby Roth introduced the Product Liability Fairness Act on May 3, 1993, and it was referred jointly to the House Committees on Energy and Commerce and Judiciary [S1][S5].

Within three weeks it was sent to the Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law and the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
It had a single cosponsor, a House Republican, and never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any further action before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers came out ahead in the narrow sense that state product liability laws, including longer filing windows, joint liability, and punitive damages against drug and aircraft makers, remained in force. Manufacturers and insurers did not get the liability limits they sought. That said, the bill had only one cosponsor and no visible momentum, so its death reflects a lack of support more than a decisive public campaign.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers kept state tort rights

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Republicans; the Democratic-controlled committees that held the bill never acted on it, so the record shows party labels but no recorded party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have replaced fifty state liability systems with one federal rulebook featuring a two-year filing deadline, a higher bar for punitive damages, and lighter liability for non-manufacturer sellers, all of which reduce what companies pay when their products injure people [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Brand-name drug and medical device makers
industries.note: Companies whose drugs or devices were FDA-approved would be immune from punitive damages unless they withheld or misrepresented information to the agency or bribed an official, a major protection in the most heavily litigated product category [S3].

Makers of FAA-certified aircraft would escape punitive damages if they complied with certification and continuing airworthiness requirements, shielding them from large verdicts in crash and defect cases [S3].

Settlement and alternative-dispute-resolution rules would impose fee penalties on plaintiffs who reject reasonable offers and then win less at trial, shifting leverage toward insurers and corporate defendants in settlement negotiations [S3].

Shorter deadlines, damage offsets, separate punitive proceedings, and attorney-fee provisions tied to settlement offers would cut both the volume and the value of product injury cases lawyers could profitably take [S3].
